description: Two-person team mixing game development and real space data. One of us builds interactive 3D worlds, the other works with data, maps and web interfaces. We're tackling Martian Map: a layered, interactive map of a real Martian site that helps plan a safe Marswalk, combining imagery, terrain, minerals and environmental data, with an immersive 3D mode on top. Interests: Mars, 3D graphics, game design, data viz, web dev. Team is complete, but happy to chat on Space Apps Connect!
summary:
Mars Map is an interactive 3D atlas and expedition planner that connects planet-wide exploration with detailed route planning in Valles Marineris. Users can explore 2,054 named Martian features, inspect terrain and historical dust observations, and generate weather and hazard scenarios. A detailed map of Southwest Candor Chasma uses HiRISE imagery and elevation data to compare walking routes, estimate travel time, and check whether an astronaut could complete a scientific task and return with a required time reserve.
The project addresses the challenge by turning planetary datasets into an understandable planning experience. It demonstrates how terrain and changing conditions influence expedition decisions. Mars Map helps users explore these trade-offs while clearly distinguishing measured data, historical observations, and simulated conditions.
details:
Mars Map combines two connected planning environments.

The global 3D atlas lets users rotate and zoom Mars, search named landforms, filter feature categories, and inspect regional information. Map layers show surface imagery, elevation, historical dust detections, simulated weather, and generated hazards. Selected regions provide terrain information, scenario risk estimates, and Wikipedia descriptions and photographs where available. Users can also place departure and destination points to explore long-distance routes.

The detailed planner covers a 2 × 2 km area of Southwest Candor Chasma within Valles Marineris. It combines HiRISE imagery with an approximately one-metre-resolution source terrain model. Users can position a proposed base and science destination directly on the terrain, adjust weather conditions, and compare short and adaptive routes. Assessments include slopes, estimated travel time, a scientific stop, the return journey, and the required time reserve.

Users can change temperature, wind, visibility, dust, and other hazard settings or generate repeatable scenarios. This makes it possible to investigate how different conditions affect the same expedition. Colour legends explain each layer, while route assessments show why a route is recommended or why an expedition should wait.

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, WebGL, and Canvas. Python supports terrain and image preparation, while Node.js supports building and deployment. Route planning uses custom A* search. Data sources include NASA HiRISE and MOLA, ESA HRSC and OMEGA, the IAU/USGS Gazetteer, and Wikipedia/Wikimedia.

The creative element is the connection between planetary exploration, detailed terrain inspection, and interactive “what-if” planning. We considered scientific usefulness, performance, accessibility, data resolution, uncertainty, and transparent explanations. Weather and hazard fields are scenarios, regional contours are approximate, and the radiation layer is a relative shielding proxy. The intended impact is educational: helping people understand how evidence and uncertainty shape future Mars expeditions.
